notes.text: You remove the main light-square defender, which weakens Black's pawn structure in the long run.
Black pushes c5 to attack your knight and force an early queen trade.
This starts the main line of the Berlin Endgame; most lines draw. Study Kramnik, Caruana and Carlsen.
You simply recapture the pawn on d4.
Now you capture the d4 pawn.
Black's pawn hits your rook, and the bishop on f5 now attacks your bishop on b1.
If Black takes, you recapture with the rook, get the open e-file, and your bishop pressures f7.
Black pushes c5 so the a5 knight can return to c6 without blocking the pawn.
Instead of castling, this heads for a quick queen trade, where the author thinks Black is better.
Your queen blocks the check and forces a queen trade, since Black's queen is pinned.
Your bishop is less strong here because of your e5 pawn.
You push the pawn rather than capture on c4.
You simply capture the bishop; your king is exposed for now.
The Open Ruy Lopez gives Black attacking chances, but your attack comes sooner because Black's king is still in the center.
Your bishop offers a trade of dark-squared bishops.
The c2 square is the safest and most useful spot for your light-squared bishop here.
Your knight retreats with gain of time, hitting the queen and keeping the center.
The most common move: it develops your bishop and prepares for Black's knight to leave c6.
The queen forks your knight and the e4 pawn; Black regains the pawn or wins the knight if you slip.
Black develops the light-squared bishop on a very active diagonal toward your e4 pawn.
This prepares d4; Black can go for the Marshall Attack with d5 or play d6.
You still challenge the e5 pawn with your d-pawn anyway.
You prepare a pawn break to open the file for your rook.
Black goes for an early queen trade, with check.
Black defends the pawn with f6, the main line.
Your rook steps up and attacks the over-extended pawn on d2.
You recapture with the rook to take control of the d-file.
Your knight retreats to d2, where it supports the e4 pawn again.
Black takes your knight hoping for a pawn recapture, but that would defeat your knight maneuver.
Black should take the pawn with the bishop, a sacrifice that hits g2.
Your kingside development is finished; now you try to gain an edge there by exchanging rooks.
In the solid Breyer, Black's knight retreats to b8 so it can reroute to d7.
An aggressive sideline: Black's bishop is active and targets your f2 pawn.
Black won't give up the center without a fight, so the e5 pawn meets yours.
Black's knight escapes to g5, though your bishop can trade it for the dark-squared bishop.
Black simply gets the king out of the center.
Qd4 forks your knight and e4 pawn, but with your king safe, simply retreat the knight.
Black goes for the attack anyway, and the bishop hits your bishop on e3.
Taking on d5 is considered the best move according to the engine.
Taking the knight with your queen is a mistake: Black's light bishop simply captures it.
Black reinforces the c5 pawn with b6, along with the dark-squared bishop.
d4 is best: it supports your rook on e5 and opens the way to develop your pieces.
The Exchange Variation: you take the knight, which defends the center, and double Black's pawns at once.
Your e5 pawn creates central tension and hits the f6 knight.
You free c2 for the bishop, a thematic Ruy Lopez idea that adds pressure on the knight.
Black has to retake with the d-pawn.
Black supports the e5 pawn and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.
Your queen takes the c-file and pressures the weak c7 pawn.
Your knight challenges the strong knight on e4; this is the St. Petersburg Variation.
Theory ends here; the position is equal and both sides have fighting chances.
Black's a-pawn heads for a4 to kick your knight off b3.
Trading off Black's light-squared bishop weakens Black's light squares.
Your knight takes the critical d4 square, hoping for an exchange that adds a defender to e5.
Black castles, getting the king out of the center.
This is the Marshall Attack, a popular, aggressive line that gives Black fighting chances.
A very common line: you still need to develop your queenside, and central control will matter.
Black's knight defends the e5 pawn.
Another Exchange Variation: you challenge the center at once and plan an early queen trade.
Suppose Black decides to capture on b3 anyway.
Black wants a well-centralized structure, not the pawn; now you can strike back and retake on e5.
You prepare to bring your bishop to c2.
This is not the best move: the bishop is less useful on b7 than on c8.
Black develops the bishop to d7; b7 would be less useful with the knight staying on c6.
This retreat is very common after Black's bishop goes to g4.
Black's queen puts long-term pressure on your weak e5 and b3 pawns.
d5 is your best move: it closes down the center.
Black trades queens early to reach a smoother endgame.
You recapture, then continue with the usual Marshall moves: queen to d3, knight to d2, and so on.
Black's bishop guards the d2 pawn.
This is the second most common move here.
Black continues by bringing the rook into the attack.
Your knight steps out of the pressure coming from Black's rook.
In the Arkhangelsk, Black builds a lot of pressure on your e4 pawn.
You keep your bishop by moving it out of danger instead of trading it.
Your setup is ideal: both knights are well placed and your bishops stare at the kingside.
Your h3 shows your kingside pawn majority and the plan to advance those pawns.
Black's pawn hits your b3 pawn, so you have to push it.
You recapture on d4, and must now avoid creating any further weaknesses.
Your h3 prepares to push your kingside pawns forward.
Black must recapture the bishop; from here you have several options, mostly developing a knight.
Your d-pawn supports e4, opens the bishop's diagonal and gives your knight two squares.
Taking the rook with the knight is a mistake: it gives away the a2 pawn.
You free your bishop from its dormant diagonal and aim for c5.
Black takes the pawn, and your pinned g-pawn can't recapture, but now you can take d2.
Black's queen develops to c7 and guards the c5 and d6 pawns.
After Nf6 you can take the e5 pawn, since Black cannot win it back safely.
Black's knight has to retreat.
A sideline: your rook guards e4 so you can push the d-pawn.
Your bishop backs up the e5 pawn and cuts the queen off from defending d3.
This stops the Marshall Attack, but you give up your opening edge; the games get complex and fun.
Beginners often play h3 to stop Qxh3, but this loses to the bishop sacrifice.
You stick to your plan, take the b-pawn and open the a-file for your rook.
The Anti-Marshall: your a-pawn hits b5, so Black must deal with it, and you avoid the heavily analysed Marshall.
Black simply develops and prepares to castle.
Your a-rook is badly placed here, and this line is rare nowadays.
Your d3 simply defends the e-pawn and sidesteps all the main theory.
Your knight had to move, or you would lose material.
Your c3 prepares to strike in the center with d4.
Black brings the rook into the game and into the attack.
Black takes the f6 pawn and pins your knight on f3 to your king.
Black is temporarily down material, but your exposed king and lack of development make Black better.
Not very common, but simple: your a-pawn hits b5 to open the file for your rook.
Black's knight attacks your bishop, wanting to trade it off and double your pawns.
Now Black's bishop is trapped and can be won later.
Black can play the Borisenko variation, putting the knight on c6 straight away.
Black's best is to take the pawn back; from here White has many ways to play.
The engine calls this equal, but Black's position is very pleasant; White avoids it and most games are drawn.
Black's bishop attacks your overextended rook and prepares a dangerous attack on your king.
Black's king finally leaves the center; the study now follows only the main line.
You develop the dark-squared bishop just in time, before the knight gets kicked out.
Taking the knight is your best move, even though it costs you a rook in the long run.
You recapture, and your knight now hits the e6 bishop, Black's main light-square defender.
Black can transpose into the Keres Defense, which is covered in another chapter.
An aggressive choice: you offer a knight trade, which also indirectly hits the c6 knight, then aim for c4.
Black's knight heads for g6, where it will be more useful than on f5.
Your rook challenges the rook on d8 so Black doesn't keep control of the d-file.
Here c3 pays off: your bishop retreats to c2.
Black develops and fixes a strategic problem by reinforcing the d5 weakness.
With castling rights gone you are worse; as White, never take the e4 pawn right away.
Black gains queenside space and may push a4 to chase your knight away.
Retaking doubles your b-pawns.
Your d5 pawn chases the knight away from c6.
Black develops the light bishop and prepares to castle long.
Your pawn hits the bishop; if it takes, you can finally capture the d2 pawn.
You should take the sacrificed bishop.
Castling heads for the Berlin endgame; a sample line shows how it unfolds.
Black castles long, getting ready to open the d-file for the rook.
Black's h5 slows down your kingside pawn advance.
The main line: Nc3 develops, challenges the center, and prepares to bring your a-rook to the d-file.
Black takes the pawn and weakens your queenside, with no fear of being trapped.
Your rook protects the e4 pawn and becomes active.
This alternative takes your king out of the pin.
Your h-pawn takes g4 away, so Black's bishop can never come there, which also stops the Marshall.
The Chigorin: Black's knight chases your bishop, then c5 and a return to c6 build a stronger center.
You stick to your plan and take the b-pawn anyway, opening the a-file for your rook.
Black's d6 supports the e5 pawn and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.
You shouldn't trade queens just yet.
Black's f-pawn backs up the knight on e4 instead of retreating it.
If Black takes the e4 pawn, you are simply better.
Black brings the rook to the center and avoids any rook exchange.
Here the Closed Ruy Lopez splits into many variations, and the position is equal.
You take the free pawn on e5 and gain control of the center.
Black ignores your threat and takes the knight, now threatening a discovered check and a dangerous attack.
Black takes the d4 pawn, challenging your center.
The position is fairly even, and most top games from here end in a draw.
Black's queen takes a more active diagonal on b7 and avoids any discovered attack.
You probably want to reroute the knight to g3 again, and this opens your bishop's diagonal.
Black castles long so the rook takes the d-file, hitting your knight on d1.
Black attacks your active bishop on a4 with the b-pawn.
Putting the rook back on e1 is the best thing you can do.
This is the original Marshall Attack, but it is inferior because the knight move blocks in the bishop.
You should obviously recapture the knight.
Black grabs the pawn and centralizes the knight.
Black moves the bishop out of danger onto an active diagonal.
You lead in development and Black can't castle, but your e5 pawn is weak. Good moves: Rd1+, h3, Nc3.
Black gains kingside space and kicks your dark-squared bishop with the g-pawn.
Black takes the chance to finally remove your light-squared bishop.
You retreat the bishop to c2 so it isn't traded for Black's misplaced knight on a5.
Black takes the rook rather than let you take control of the file.
Taking with the f-pawn is your only move.
Black must play g6, or your knight jumps to f5.
The g6 move also opens the diagonal for Black's bishop on f8.
You simply recapture the bishop with your rook.
Castling heads for the Berlin Endgame.
To play for a win instead, push your d-pawn to d3.
If Black grabs the pawn, Re1 pins the queen to the king and wins it.
You had to retreat the knight, or Black would win material.
Black is a bit more active because you never castled; castling was better, but this is still playable.
You simply develop another piece with this knight move.
Retaking with the knight is your only sensible move, unless you want to play without a queen.
This is the most common move here.
c6 is Black's best: it guards the knight on d5 against your rook and bishop.
Your only legal move is to take back the queen with the king.
Your knight hits the e4 pawn; Black is active, but you are slightly better.
You leave the pin for now and plan to reroute the knight to g3, a common Ruy Lopez idea.
Black's passed pawn on d3 now attacks your bishop on c2.
Black exchanges the knights.
Black's queen takes back the pawn with check.
Black pins your knight to the king and indirectly pressures e4; the position is fairly equal.
You develop again and reinforce your e4 pawn.
Black hits your e5 pawn and wants to open the f-file as soon as possible.
Taking d2 ends the pressure from that pawn and adds defenders to your knight on d6.
In the Chigorin, Black's knight attacks your bishop on b3 and prepares c5.
Black's knight and bishop both hit your c5 bishop, threatening to win a piece.
Grabbing the e5 pawn is dubious: Black's queen fork wins the pawn right back.
Black simply takes the pawn, and it now hits your knight on c3.
Black's knight adds a second attacker against your pinned knight on f3.
Your c3 prepares d4 and gives your bishop a retreat to c2.
This is the Gligoric main line: you lead in development, but your a1 rook is stuck.
You develop your knight further.
Black takes back on e5 and invites a knight trade, so the d-pawn can support the center again.
Black's best reply is simply to take the pawn.
Black's knight removes a defender of the e5 pawn and threatens several of your pieces.
Taking back on d4 isn't advised; move your knight to a more useful square instead.
This is the Bernstein Variation, your most common move: you want to get rid of the e4 knight.
Your bishop lands on c2 and adds pressure on the e4 knight.
Black must defend the e5 pawn, most commonly with f6.
Your rook hits the knight on e5, aiming to drive it away.
This is the Arkhangelsk: Black risks the king in the centre for rapid development and an active bishop.
Black's pawn attacks your knight, forcing it to move.
Black can strike with d5 instead of c5, putting tension on your e4 pawn.
This is the Breyer: Black reroutes the knight to d7, where it defends e5.
Your h-pawn stops Black's bishop from reaching g4.
Your plan: push d4, then bring the b1 knight around to g3.
The Marshall Attack: Black strikes at your e4 pawn at once, the most aggressive weapon against the Ruy Lopez.
Your bishop has to retreat.
Your c3 pawn frees the c2 square, a much safer diagonal for your bishop.
Things calm down here; this is 18 moves of theory, which you must know to play the Ruy Lopez well.
Black finally castles and gets the king out of the center.
Black's bishop is free again; taking c3 is fine, but your overextended pawns leave Black better.
Black skips taking on b3, develops simply and prepares to castle.
This looks nothing like the Marshall; it is very close to the Arkhangelsk with the bishop on the long diagonal.
Black's a-pawn gains queenside space and hits your knight on b3.
The Berlin Defense is one of Black's best answers to the Ruy Lopez, made famous by Kramnik against Kasparov.
Your rook supports the d3 bishop and helps stop a queenside pawn break.
Black centralizes the queen behind the light-squared bishop, forming a battery.
Your b3 leads to a fianchetto: the bishop goes to b2.
Moving the bishop away is the only sensible move for you.
Your rook adds a defender to the e5 pawn, undermining Black's pressure on it.
Black's rook joins the b-file behind the queen, adding a defender for the b5 pawn.
You castle to get your king out of the center; Re1 will then support the e-pawn.
Retaking gives up your opening edge; a sample line shows how level it gets.
Your bishop reaches c5 and threatens to capture the rook on f8.
Black can take the pawn at once instead of playing queen c7 first, then develop the bishop.
Black's rook leaves danger. The position is roughly equal, but Black's kingside attack means you must play carefully.
Black develops the bishop before solidifying e5, since Bxc6 can sometimes threaten to win that pawn.
Black retreats the knight and seems to threaten your bishop, but taking it is not necessarily good.
You continue with the pawn break by capturing on b5.
This is basically your only move here: you challenge the center at once.
Most Arkhangelsk games reach this position, and you have several options from here.
Black's queen and bishop bear down on h2; g3 is your only move that holds.
Black should just accept the queen trade.
Retreating to a4 is the most common choice and keeps the pressure on the c6 knight.
This is the Open Ruy Lopez: Black grabs the e4 pawn, risky but with enough resources; you strike back in the center.
The a2 pawn looks free, but you can trap the bishop with b3.
The theory mostly ends here; you have three main moves, all played about equally often.
Black keeps reinforcing the center; this main line goes on for a long time without branching.
Black's bishop reinforces the passed pawn on d3.
If Black takes the pawn, you are much better: play Re1, then trade off the light-squared bishop.
The bishop retreats to b1, the only open square, and keeps pressure on the d3 pawn.
Black sacrifices two minor pieces for a rook and a pawn; this Dilworth Variation is equal after the exchanges.
Your knight returns to b3 and adds pressure on the d4 pawn.
Your knight goes to d6, probably its most useful and safest square.
Your d4 pawn keeps fighting for the center while Black's king is still on e8.
This is the third most common move, and the best one according to the engine.
Once more, the e5 pawn is a drawback for you.
Qd6 is another way for Black to defend the e5 pawn, besides f6.
Black improves the pawn structure but gives up the main defender of the light squares.
This is the main starting position of the Breyer, the best line for both sides.
Black's rook goes to e8, reinforcing the e-file and the center.
Black retreats the knight back to a5.
Black simply develops and centralizes the queen.
Black's queen attacks your weak knight on f5 and prepares to go to g6.
Castling accepts that the game may head into the Berlin Endgame.
Black expects h4: after the bishop takes, your g-pawn is pinned, but you still win the d2 pawn.
You take on d4 and offer a queen trade.
Black's a-pawn challenges your bishop; you can take on c6 or retreat to a4.
Bg4 is another option for Black instead of f6.
You answer by challenging the center yourself with d4, hitting the e5 pawn.
Black's best option: taking the pawn removes your central threat.
Black develops the bishop to prepare castling; this begins the Closed Ruy Lopez.
Black wins the pawn back and opens the a-file for a rook trade.
Your bishop on e3 covers c5 and stops Black's dangerous attack with Bc5.
The Open Ruy Lopez gives Black chances, but you can attack sooner while Black's king sits in the center.
Black can also develop the bishop to b7 straight away instead of playing queen c7.
Black centralizes the queen and lines it up with the bishop; the position is about even.
You simply recapture the pawn.
Taking Black's bishop on g4 would allow mate in two, so don't.
Theory ends here: Black's bishop eyes your knight, so understand each move and play with your own ideas.
Your knight heads for d4 rather than capturing the f-pawn en passant.
You are slightly better, though both sides still have chances; taking the e-pawn is not Black's best.
You simply develop your dark-squared bishop.
Black takes your knight and threatens your rook; recapture with the pawn, since taking with the queen would be costly.
Your rook goes to c1 to support the c-file; both sides are regrouping their pieces.
Retaking with the queen is not advised; you are better here than after the bishop retake.
Your knight reaches d4, as planned.
Your bishop develops and puts pressure on the c7 pawn.
Your bishop retreats to b3 and eyes the f7 pawn; it usually ends up on c2.
Black's f-pawn backs up the e5 pawn to reinforce the center.
You hold a pawn majority on the kingside and plan to develop rapidly.
This pawn attacks your bishop and prepares ...d5.
If White still tries to trap the bishop, Black simply pushes the c-pawn.
Black swings the rook to h6 to join the game. Never capture on e6.
The most common move, aiming at development; Black should never take this bishop.
Your bishop leaves c2, opening the file for your rook and hitting the b5 pawn.
Black attacks your c3 pawn to win more central squares for the knight.
Your d4 challenges the center, hitting c5 and e5, the move you have prepared all along.
Your a-pawn eyes b5 to undermine Black's pawns and prepare a break that opens the a-file.
Your bishop pressures the c6 knight; this is the start of the Ruy Lopez.
Black's c5 adds pressure on the center and frees c6 for the knight to return.
Your rook takes the e-file and protects the e4 pawn, reaching the Closed Ruy Lopez.
You develop the bishop, ready for Re1 when Black pushes the pawn to d2.
Black finally castles and is ready to start an attack.
Black naturally recaptures the bishop.
Black wants the queen trade, so the c-pawn attacks your knight on d4.
You finally win the pawn back on e5.
Nxd4 is the main line; avoid trading queens if you can, though a trade would not hurt you.
Your knight again tries to chase Black's knight away from e4.
Black develops the bishop and prepares to castle long.
Black keeps the queen in the attack and eyes g2; you have four common ways to defend.
Taking on d4 gives your e5 pawn another defender.
Black simply develops a piece.
Your e-pawn stakes a claim in the center, controlling d5 and f5.
Take the f-pawn to create a weakness on Black's kingside too.
Your bishop gets ready to kick the knight out of e4.
Black's pawn stops Rh4 from expelling the queen; don't take it with the bishop, or Qf5 forks.
d4 is your only really good move; it hits e5 now that Black's knight has left c6.
Black recaptures the bishop with the rook.
Black grabs your e4 pawn, a slightly risky choice; answer by striking in the center yourself.
You simply get your bishop out of danger.
You have to retake with the king here, for a long-term reason shown later.
Black's knight finally returns to c6, following its original plan.
The main alternative to the Berlin: d3 supports your e4 pawn, so Black can't capture it.
Black's pawn attacks your bishop and forces it to retreat.
This is the Closed Ruy Lopez: Black develops instead of taking e4, and the position is fairly equal.
A good beginner trap: the queen is pinned to the king, so Black must take the rook.
You simply trade knights on e5.
The Exchange Variation removes a defender of the center and doubles Black's pawns; you rely on your kingside majority.
The second most common move: your a-pawn controls b4, so Black's knight gets no outpost there.
Your queen moves to e2, a more useful square.
Black simply develops, heading to castle.
Black's bishop adds pressure on your e4 pawn.
Black's bishop puts long-term pressure on your knight.
Black castles, and trading on e4 doesn't work yet because the d-pawn would then hit your f3 knight.
Black has to recapture, and you are considerably better.
Reroute the knight to f5 via f1 and g3, develop the bishop to e3, and put a rook on c1.
Your knight steps to b3, but your dark-squared bishop still needs developing.
An alternative: your bishop gets the safer, more active c2 diagonal, but this allows Black's Bc5.
Your knight returns to f3, a much more useful square.
Capture the bishop first, before dealing with the d4 pawn.
Your a-pawn attacks the b5 pawn, and you want to trade rooks.
You recapture the knight, and the a-file opens for your rook.
Black gets a swift attack as compensation: your pieces are undeveloped and your bishop on b3 is nearly useless.
Retreating the knight to f3 is your only move, and it hits the queen.
The position is fairly even; you plan a kingside attack, while Black has a queenside pawn majority.
You happily trade bishops, because Black's dark squares become much more vulnerable.
Black has three replies here: Be7, Be6 or h5, with h5 the main one.
Your knight develops and attacks the e5 pawn.
This is the second most popular move after Qh4.
This quiet pawn move prepares h4, to drive the bishop off its diagonal.
Your knight leaves the attack and opens the door to a queen trade.
Not recommended: Black can take on e4 and hit your f3 knight, which guards e5. Not exactly bad, though.
Black develops the knight and pressures your e4 pawn.
Luckily you can retake the queen with the knight instead of the king.
Black's bishop eyes your rook on d1 and will take it unless you react.
Black simply recaptures the knight.
Black also sticks to the plan and trades the knight for your bishop; you must retake.
Black's knight reaches d7; now Black wants c5, Re8, Bf8 and Bb7, and both sides finish their plans.
Black plays Bc5 to control an important diagonal; this is the Italian Variation.
The bishops may be exchanged; this resembles closed Ruy Lopez lines, nothing like the Marshall Attack.
Black regains the pawn with check, and you must trade queens or end up much worse.
Don't take the e5 pawn: Black's queen move wins it back, so just develop normally.
Black's bishop hits your queen with tempo; the book answer is Qd3.
You go ahead with the rook exchange.
Black simply develops the knight.
Black finally plays the c5 move it prepared, hitting your d4 pawn.
Your f-pawn hits the knight, indirectly defending e5; if the queen takes e5 later, a fork follows.
g3 is the only move that doesn't lose: it hits the queen and shuts the bishop's diagonal.
Black simply develops and will castle to get the king out of the center.
Black's bishop takes your rook with check, completing the exchange.
You finally start the exchange by taking the e7 bishop.
You have several good options here.
You challenge the center at once, hitting the e5 pawn, since d5 isn't yet possible for Black.
Black gets the king out of the center.
